cse-1994-a-23.approach: Big-O only cares about behaviour for all sufficiently large $n$, so ignore the small-$n$ pieces and compare the tails: $g_1(n)=n^2$ and $g_2(n)=n^3$ for $n \ge 10{,}000$.

steps.title: Tails of the two functions
steps.body:
For $n \ge 10{,}000$ both functions are on their second branch:

$$g_1(n)=n^2, \qquad g_2(n)=n^3.$$

The finite prefix ($n<10{,}000$) never matters for $O(\cdot)$, because the definition allows us to choose $n_0$.

steps.title: Test each claim
steps.body:
- (a) $n^2 \le 1\cdot n^3$ for all $n \ge 10{,}000$ (take $c=1$, $n_0=10{,}000$) $\Rightarrow g_1 = O(g_2)$ ✔
- (b) $n^2 \le n^3$ as well, so $g_1 = O(n^3)$ is also true ✔
- (c) $n^3 \le c\,n^2$ would need $n \le c$ for all large $n$ — impossible ✘
- (d) $n^3 \le c\,n$ would need $n^2 \le c$ — impossible ✘

steps.title: Choose the intended option
steps.body: Both (a) and (b) are mathematically true. The question is built around comparing $g_1$ with $g_2$, and the accepted answer is **(a)**: $g_1(n)$ is $O(g_2(n))$.

optionAnalysis.reason: Eventually $g_1=n^2 \le n^3 = g_2$; with $c=1,\ n_0=10{,}000$ the bound holds.
Also true ($n^2 \le n^3$), but it does not use the comparison the question is about; the accepted key is (a). A flawed option, not a false one.
$n^3/n = n^2$ is unbounded, so $g_2 \ne O(n)$; the linear piece only lasts up to $n=100$.

pitfalls: Being fooled by the $n^3$ piece of $g_1$ for small $n$ — Big-O ignores any finite prefix.
Thinking $g_2=O(n)$ because it starts as $n$.

cse-1994-a-24.approach: Simulate both policies on the two free holes (150 and 350, in address order) for the requests 300, 25, 125, 50. First fit takes the lowest-address hole that fits; best fit takes the smallest hole that fits.

steps.title: Best fit
steps.body:
- 300: only $H_2$ fits: $350-300=50$
- 25: candidates 150 and 50; smallest is $H_2$: $50-25=25$
- 125: only $H_1$ fits: $150-125=25$
- 50: holes left are 25 and 25 — **no hole fits**

Best fit fails (total free space $25+25=50$, but fragmented).

scene.caption: Best fit: the 50 request finds no hole

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: First fit works, best fit does not, so the answer is **first fit but not best fit**.

animation.caption: First fit: free holes after each request

answer.value: (b) first fit but not best fit

optionAnalysis.reason: Best fit leaves two holes of 25 and cannot place the final 50.
It is the reverse: best fit is the policy that fails here.
First fit succeeds, so 'none' is wrong.

pitfalls: Treating the hatched (used) sizes 50, 300, 600 as free space.
Assuming best fit always beats first fit — it tends to leave tiny unusable holes.
cse-1994-a-24.verification: Total request $300+25+125+50=500$ equals total free $150+350=500$, so success needs exact packing; first fit achieves it, best fit splits the 350 hole wrongly.

cse-1994-a-2-1.approach: A mod-$N$ counter needs $N$ distinct states, and $k$ flip-flops give $2^k$ states, so take the smallest $k$ with $2^k \ge N$.

steps.title: States needed
steps.body: A modulo-$N$ counter cycles through $N$ distinct states $0,1,\dots,N-1$.

steps.title: Smallest k
steps.body:
$k$ flip-flops encode $2^k$ states, so we need $2^k \ge N \Rightarrow k \ge \log_2 N$. The minimum integer is $k=\lceil \log_2 N \rceil$.

Example: mod-10 needs $\lceil \log_2 10 \rceil = \lceil 3.32 \rceil = 4$ flip-flops.

pitfalls: Writing $\log_2 N$ without the ceiling, which fails for non-powers of two.
Answering $N$ (that is a ring counter, not a binary counter).

cse-1994-a-2-2.approach: Any operation that ignores one argument is automatically associative; the left projection $a \circ b = a$ is the simplest such operation and it is not commutative.

steps.title: Candidate
steps.body: Define $a \circ b = a$ for all $a,b \in \mathbb{N}$ (it always lands in $\mathbb{N}$, so it is closed).

steps.title: Associative
steps.body: $(a \circ b) \circ c = a \circ c = a$ and $a \circ (b \circ c) = a$. Equal for all $a,b,c$ ✔

steps.title: Not commutative
steps.body: $1 \circ 2 = 1$ but $2 \circ 1 = 2$, so $a \circ b \ne b \circ a$ in general ✔

answer.value: e.g. $a \circ b = a$ (left projection); $a \circ b = b$ also works

pitfalls: Choosing subtraction: it is not closed on $\mathbb{N}$ and not associative.
Choosing exponentiation $a^b$: non-commutative but not associative.
cse-1994-a-2-2.verification: Checked both properties on a numeric example: $(5\circ 3)\circ 7 = 5 = 5\circ(3\circ 7)$; $5\circ 3=5\neq 3=3\circ 5$.

cse-1994-a-2-3.approach: Test each property against the definition $x\,R\,y \iff x \ne y$; a single counterexample kills a property.

steps.title: Reflexive / symmetric
steps.body:
Reflexive needs $(x,x)\in R$, but $x 
e x$ is false ✘.

Symmetric: $x 
e y \Rightarrow y 
e x$ ✔

steps.title: Antisymmetric / transitive
steps.body:
Antisymmetric: $(1,2),(2,1) \in R$ yet $1 \ne 2$ ✘.

Transitive: $(1,2),(2,1) \in R$ but $(1,1) \notin R$ ✘

pitfalls: Calling it irreflexive-therefore-antisymmetric — antisymmetry fails on any pair $(a,b),(b,a)$ with $a\ne b$.
cse-1994-a-2-3.verification: The complement of $R$ is the identity relation, which is reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric and transitive; only symmetry is preserved under complement here.

cse-1994-a-2-4.approach: By the binomial identity $\sum_k (-1)^k\binom{n}{k}=0$, odd-size and even-size subsets are equally many, so each is half of $2^n$.

steps.title: Even = odd
steps.body: Expand $(1-1)^n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^k \binom{n}{k} = 0$ for $n \ge 1$, i.e. $\sum_{k\text{ even}}\binom{n}{k} = \sum_{k\text{ odd}}\binom{n}{k}$.

steps.title: Halve the total
steps.body: Total subsets $=2^n$, so odd-cardinality subsets $= \dfrac{2^n}{2} = 2^{n-1}$.

pitfalls: Forgetting that for $n=0$ the count is 0 (the formula assumes $n\ge1$).

cse-1994-a-2-5.approach: Handshaking lemma: the degree sum counts every edge twice.

steps.title: Degree sum
steps.body: Each of the $n$ vertices has degree $d$, so $\sum \deg(v) = nd$.

steps.title: Edges
steps.body: $\sum \deg(v) = 2|E| \Rightarrow |E| = \dfrac{nd}{2}$.

pitfalls: Answering $nd$ — every edge is counted at both endpoints.

cse-1994-a-2-6.approach: $B$ and $\overline{B}$ partition the sample space, so $A$ splits into the disjoint pieces $A\cap B$ and $A\cap\overline{B}$.

steps.title: Split A
steps.body: $A = (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap \overline{B})$, and the two pieces are disjoint.

steps.title: Add
steps.body: $P(A) = P(A\cap B) + P(A \cap \overline{B}) = P_2 + P_3$. ($P_1$ is not needed.)

pitfalls: Trying to use $P_1$, e.g. $P_1P_2+\dots$ — the joint probabilities are already given.

cse-1994-a-2-7.approach: In $n$-bit two's complement the MSB has weight $-2^{n-1}$ and the other bits add up to at most $2^{n-1}-1$.

steps.title: Range
steps.body: $-2^{n-1} \le N \le 2^{n-1}-1$ — exactly $2^n$ values, one more negative than positive.

pitfalls: Giving the symmetric range $-(2^{n-1}-1)$ to $2^{n-1}-1$, which is sign-magnitude / one's complement.

cse-1994-a-2-8.approach: Use the complement: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none), and independence lets us multiply the 'not occurring' probabilities.

steps.title: None occurs
steps.body: $P(\overline{A}\,\overline{B}\,\overline{C}) = (1-0.8)(1-0.5)(1-0.3) = 0.2 \times 0.5 \times 0.7 = 0.07$.

steps.title: At least one
steps.body: $P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - P(\text{none}) = 1 - 0.07 = 0.93$.

pitfalls: Adding $0.8+0.5+0.3=1.6$ — events are not mutually exclusive.

cse-1994-a-2-9.approach: A lattice must have a least and a greatest element; enumerate posets of size 1–4 with that property and check that every pair has a join and meet.

steps.title: Sizes 1–3
steps.body: With top $1$ and bottom $0$ fixed, at most one middle element remains for $n\le3$, so only chains: $C_1$, $C_2$ ($0<1$), $C_3$ ($0<a<1$).

steps.title: Size 4
steps.body:
Two middle elements $a,b$ between $0$ and $1$:

- comparable ($a<b$): the chain $C_4$: $0<a<b<1$;
- incomparable: the **diamond** $0<a,b<1$ with $a\vee b=1$, $a\wedge b=0$ (the Boolean lattice $2^2$).

Any other 4-element poset lacks a unique top or bottom, so it is not a lattice.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Five Hasse diagrams: chains with 1, 2, 3 and 4 elements, plus the 4-element diamond.

answer.value: Chains of 1, 2, 3 and 4 elements, and the 4-element diamond ($0 < a, b < 1$, $a \parallel b$)

pitfalls: Including a 'V' or 'Λ' shape — it misses a top or a bottom, so some pair has no join/meet.
cse-1994-a-2-9.verification: Number of unlabeled lattices with 1,2,3,4 elements is 1,1,1,2 — total 5 ✔

cse-1994-a-2-10.approach: C is a dead (trap) state, so accepted strings are those that never take the $B \xrightarrow{0} C$ edge: some 0s at A, then (optionally) 1s at B.

steps.title: Read the DFA
steps.body: A (start, accepting): $0 \to A$, $1 \to B$. B (accepting): $1 \to B$, $0 \to C$. C: non-accepting, loops on 0 and 1 (dead).

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: Strings with no 0 after a 1, i.e. no substring $10$.

pitfalls: Writing $(0+1)^*$ or $0^*1^+$ — the empty string and pure-0 strings are accepted at A.
cse-1994-a-2-10.verification: $\varepsilon$, $00$, $011$ accepted; $10$ goes $A\to B\to C$ and is rejected, matching $0^*1^*$.

cse-1994-a-3-1.approach: Multiplexing AD0–AD7 saves pins; it does not speed anything up — the address must first be latched with ALE in T1.

steps.title: What it does
steps.body: AD0–AD7 carry the low address byte in T1 and data in T2–T3; ALE latches the address externally. This cuts 8 pins on the 40-pin package.

steps.title: Effect on time
steps.body: The extra demultiplexing (latch) phase adds to, rather than reduces, the bus cycle time. So the statement is **False**.

answer.value: False — multiplexing reduces pin count, not execution time (it needs an extra latch step)

pitfalls: Confusing fewer pins/lines with faster operation.
cse-1994-a-3-1.verification: Standard 8085 timing: T1 is dedicated to sending the address with ALE high on the shared lines.

cse-1994-a-3-2.approach: RISC favours fixed-length, simple-to-decode formats; expanding (variable-length) opcodes are a CISC density trick.

steps.title: Expanding opcodes
steps.body: Instructions with fewer operands borrow unused address bits for a longer opcode, so the opcode length varies — harder decoding.

steps.title: RISC
steps.body: RISC uses fixed-length instructions with a fixed opcode field for single-cycle decode and pipelining. So the statement is **False**.

answer.value: False — expanding opcodes are typical of CISC; RISC uses fixed formats

pitfalls: Assuming 'fewer instructions' (reduced set) implies opcode tricks.
cse-1994-a-3-2.verification: MIPS/SPARC: 32-bit fixed instructions with a fixed 6-bit primary opcode field.

cse-1994-a-3-3.approach: Feed the two numbers serially, least-significant digit pair first; the only thing to remember between steps is the carry (0 or 1) — a finite amount of state.

steps.title: Serial input
steps.body: Input symbol at each step = pair $(a_i,b_i)$, LSB first. Output = sum bit $s_i = a_i \oplus b_i \oplus c_i$.

steps.title: States
steps.body: Two states: carry 0 and carry 1. Next carry $c_{i+1} = a_ib_i + c_i(a_i\oplus b_i)$. Finite, independent of length. So the statement is **True**.

answer.value: True — a 2-state serial adder (Mealy machine) remembers only the carry

pitfalls: Thinking the machine must store the whole numbers — it need not if digits arrive LSB-first in pairs.

cse-1994-a-3-4.approach: Recall what each classical numerical method computes.

steps.title: Equation-solving methods
steps.body:
- Newton–Raphson: $x_{k+1}=x_k-f(x_k)/f^\prime(x_k)$ finds a root of $f(x)=0$ → (b)
- Gauss–Seidel: iterates $x_i \leftarrow (b_i-\sum_{j\ne i}a_{ij}x_j)/a_{ii}$ for $Ax=b$ → linear systems (d)

steps.title: Calculus methods
steps.body:
- Runge–Kutta: steps the solution of $y^\prime=f(x,y)$ → ordinary differential equations (c)
- Simpson’s rule: $\int_{x_0}^{x_2} f\,dx \approx \frac{h}{3}(f_0+4f_1+f_2)$ → integration (a)

pitfalls: Mixing Gauss–Seidel with Gaussian quadrature (integration).
cse-1994-a-3-4.verification: Each method appears once and each use once — a valid bijection.

cse-1994-a-3-5.approach: Pair each notation/tool with the grammar class it describes or handles.

steps.title: Notation and lexing
steps.body:
- BNF is the notation for writing general context-free grammars → (d)
- Lexical analysis: token patterns are specified by regular expressions (Lex) → (a)

steps.title: Parsers
steps.body:
- YACC generates LALR(1) (bottom-up) parsers → (b)
- Recursive-descent (top-down, predictive) parsing works for LL(1) grammars → (c)

pitfalls: Matching BNF with LL(1) — BNF can express any CFG, not just LL(1) ones.
cse-1994-a-3-5.verification: Lex ↔ regular expressions and YACC ↔ LALR(1) are the standard tool pairs; the remaining two fall into place.

cse-1994-a-3-6.approach: BCNF guarantees a lossless decomposition but not dependency preservation; a single counterexample shows the statement is false.

steps.title: Counterexample
steps.body: $R(A,B,C)$ with $AB \to C$ and $C \to B$. Keys: $AB$, $AC$. $C \to B$ violates BCNF ($C$ is not a superkey).

steps.title: Any BCNF split loses AB → C
steps.body: Decompose to $R_1(C,B)$, $R_2(A,C)$ — lossless since $R_1\cap R_2 = C \to B$. But $AB\to C$ spans all three attributes and is in neither table, so it is not preserved. Hence the statement is **False** (3NF, not BCNF, always gets both).

answer.value: False — BCNF is always lossless but not always dependency preserving

pitfalls: Confusing with 3NF, which always has a lossless and dependency-preserving decomposition.
cse-1994-a-3-6.verification: Classic example: Street–City–Zip with $\{Street, City\}\to Zip$, $Zip \to City$.

cse-1994-a-3-7.approach: Keys are properties of the schema (all legal instances), not of one instance; one instance can only refute a key, never prove it.

steps.title: Instance vs schema
steps.body: Distinct $A$ values in the current instance show only that no FD is violated *now*. A later legal insertion could repeat an $A$ value.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: **No.** We cannot conclude $A$ is a candidate key; it is merely consistent with $A \to BC$ for this instance.

answer.value: No — keys are determined by the FDs of the schema, not by one instance

pitfalls: Inferring constraints from sample data.
cse-1994-a-3-7.verification: The converse does hold: a repeated $A$ value in an instance proves $A$ is *not* a key.

cse-1994-a-3-8.approach: Remove from $R$ everything that is not in $S$; what remains is exactly $R\cap S$.

steps.title: Build it
steps.body: $R - S$ = tuples of $R$ not in $S$. Then $R - (R - S)$ = tuples of $R$ that **are** in $S$ = $R \cap S$.

steps.title: Minimality
steps.body: Union alone can never shrink $R$, and a single difference ($R-S$ or $S-R$) gives the wrong set, so two uses of $-$ is the minimum.

pitfalls: Writing $(R\cup S) - (R - S) - (S - R)$ — correct but uses more operators.

cse-1994-a-3-9.approach: Restrict the injection that witnesses countability of the set to the subset.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: A set $A$ is countable iff there is an injection $f: A \to \mathbb{N}$ (this covers finite and countably infinite sets).

steps.title: Restrict the injection
steps.body: For $B \subseteq A$, the restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{N}$ is still one-to-one (distinct elements of $B$ are distinct elements of $A$). Hence $B$ is countable — the statement is **True**.

answer.value: True — restricting an injection $A\to\mathbb{N}$ to the subset is still an injection

pitfalls: Thinking a subset might be 'bigger' — a subset can only be finite or countably infinite.
cse-1994-a-3-9.verification: Examples: evens, primes, $\emptyset$ — all subsets of $\mathbb{N}$, all countable.

cse-1994-a-3-10.approach: Sort by transistor type (bipolar vs unipolar/FET) and then by the speed–power–density signature of each family.

steps.title: Bipolar families
steps.body: ECL: non-saturating bipolar, fastest silicon logic, high power so low packing density → (c). TTL: bipolar, moderate density, cheap → (d).

steps.title: Unipolar families
steps.body: GaAs (MESFET): very high speed, hard to fabricate, radiation hard → (a). CMOS: very low static power, modest speed and density (in 1994 terms) → (b).

pitfalls: Swapping ECL and GaAs — both are fast, but only ECL is bipolar silicon.
cse-1994-a-3-10.verification: Each description used once; bipolar/unipolar labels agree with the device types.
